parts.title: Renal cortex
parts.description: The outer layer. It contains structures where blood filtration begins.

parts.title: Renal medulla
parts.description: The inner region. Its tubules help concentrate urine and recover water and substances the body needs.

parts.title: Glomerulus
parts.description: A small cluster of vessels acting as a filter. Water and waste pass through; large proteins usually stay in the blood.

parts.title: Ureter
parts.description: The tube carrying urine from the kidney to the bladder. It does not carry blood.

parts.title: Renal artery
parts.description: The vessel supplying blood to the kidney. High glucose and blood pressure can damage small vessels in the filtration system.

filterStages.title: A barrier that selects.
filterStages.description: With preserved filtration, water and small molecules pass through. Blood cells and most large proteins remain in circulation.

filterStages.title: Small vessels face pressure.
filterStages.description: Sustained high glucose and elevated pressure can affect filter structures. There may be no symptoms at first.

filterStages.title: Some proteins may pass through.
filterStages.description: When the barrier changes, urine albumin may increase. A test measures it; looking at urine cannot confirm it.

filterStages.title: Filtration may decrease.
filterStages.description: If damage progresses, the kidney may remove less waste. Repeated tests and clinical context assess progression; care and treatment may slow it.

sections.title: Why can kidney damage occur?
sections.description: Diabetic kidney disease is kidney damage related to type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Long-term high glucose can affect the kidney’s small blood vessels.
points: More years with diabetes and sustained high glucose.
High blood pressure, cholesterol and triglycerides.
Age, family history of kidney disease and previous kidney injury.
Smoking, inactivity, excess salt and obesity.
sections.note: Risk can be reduced: managing glucose and blood pressure, following treatment and attending checkups helps protect the kidneys.

sections.title: Prevention starts with context.
sections.description: Kidney disease is an important diabetes complication worldwide. Risk varies with diabetes duration, age, glucose control, blood pressure, weight and blood lipids.
points: Comparing countries requires knowing the population, year and disease definition.
Draft figures are displayed pending verification.
A population statistic does not predict an individual’s progression.
sections.note: Not everyone with diabetes develops kidney damage. Statistics help study the issue; checkups guide personal care.

sections.title: Daily care can make a difference.
sections.description: Early detection and diabetes management can prevent or delay complications. Damage can develop slowly without obvious signs.
sections.pointsTitle: Care to agree on with your team
points: Glucose and pressure: know your targets and monitor as advised.
Medicines: follow prescribed treatment and ask before making changes.
Avoid tobacco and vaping; seek support to quit.
Adapted activity: one possible goal is 30 minutes on 5 days. Include strength work if advised.
Food and fluids: review salt and adapt amounts to your results.
Checkups: ask about yearly tests for type 2 diabetes and after 5 years of type 1 diabetes, or sooner if advised.
sections.note: This is not an absolute guarantee of prevention. Testing frequency, exercise and targets must be adapted to each person.

sections.title: Tests are part of the answer.
sections.description: Early stages can have few or no symptoms. Blood and urine tests help assess how the kidneys work.
points: Blood: creatinine helps the laboratory estimate glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Urine: the albumin/creatinine ratio helps assess protein loss.
The team interprets repeated results alongside clinical history.
Thirst and frequent urination can accompany diabetes; they do not confirm kidney damage.
sections.note: Swelling, changes in urine or tiredness need assessment. General diabetes symptoms should not be confused with confirmation of kidney disease.

infoGlossaryTitle: Words you will hear at your appointment.

infoGlossary.def: Kidney damage related to diabetes. It usually progresses slowly and silently.
A cluster of tiny kidney vessels that filters the blood.
A protein that normally stays in the blood. If it persistently appears in urine, it may point to filter damage.
A muscle waste product measured in blood. The lab uses it to estimate eGFR.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate: a calculation of how well the kidneys filter. Your health team interprets it.
A urine test that helps assess protein loss.
A test that reflects average glucose over the last few months.
The force of blood against the arteries. It is written as two numbers (systolic/diastolic) in mmHg.
A condition in which diabetes damages the kidneys over time, making it harder for them to filter waste and extra fluid from the blood.
A condition in which the kidneys have damage or reduced function that lasts for at least three months.
A long-term condition in which blood sugar levels are too high because the body does not make enough insulin or cannot use insulin properly.
Health problems caused by damage to the body’s smallest blood vessels. Diabetes can cause these complications in the eyes, kidneys, and nerves.
A condition in which the body’s immune system attacks the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. People with type 1 diabetes need insulin to manage their blood sugar.

The most common type of diabetes. The body makes insulin but does not use it well (insulin resistance) and, over time, may make less of it. It is linked to age, excess weight, low physical activity and family history. It is managed with diet, physical activity, medicines and sometimes insulin.

infoGlossary.def: When the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood is higher than normal.
A condition in which excess body fat can affect a person’s health.
When blood pushes against the walls of the blood vessels with persistently elevated force. Also called hypertension.
A group of conditions that affect the heart or blood vessels.
When levels of fats in the blood, such as cholesterol or triglycerides, are outside the healthy range.
Albumin (a protein) in the urine: it means protein is leaking into the urine.
Protein in the urine in a higher amount than normal. It includes albumin and other proteins. If it persists over time, it may point to kidney damage.

When the kidneys get damaged more easily than usual, for example because of age, family history, or having diabetes, high blood pressure and other risk factors at the same time.

learn.label: Epidemiology
learn.title: A common complication.
learn.draft: ajustado por el equipo de diseño (v4.6), por validar

blocks.heading: What is it?
paragraphs: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is one of the most common complications of diabetes. Over time, high blood sugar levels can damage the small blood vessels in the kidneys, making it harder for them to filter waste from the blood. Globally, diabetes is one of the leading causes of chronic kidney disease (CKD), and DKD occurs in approximately 20–40% of people with diabetes.
For people with type 1 diabetes, DKD can occur several years later. In contrast, people with type 2 diabetes may already have DKD when their diabetes is diagnosed.

The risk of developing DKD increases with age and with the length of time a person has had diabetes. People with type 2 diabetes are also at greater risk. Other risk factors include obesity, high blood sugar, abnormal blood fat levels, high blood pressure, or having a cardiovascular disease. Together, these factors can increase the risk of kidney damage. Sex differences exist, but studies have found different results depending on factors such as population and age.

blocks.heading: What about in Mexico?
paragraphs: In Mexico, kidney disease is a major public health concern due to the high rates of diabetes and other cardiovascular risk factors. National data estimate that 16.8% of adults in Mexico have diabetes, while only about 42% of those with diabetes have their blood sugar levels under control. It is estimated that about 14 million Mexicans live with chronic kidney disease (CKD) from any cause, diagnosed or not, with diabetes being one of the most significant causes. It is also estimated that 1 out of every 4 people who live with diabetes develop DKD.

paragraphs: Diabetic kidney disease, also known as diabetic nephropathy, is a complication of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and it has many causes at once (its origin is multifactorial).

The main cause is long exposure to diabetes, especially when blood sugar is not well controlled. According to global estimates, 20–40% of people with diabetes develop diabetic kidney disease (see Epidemiology).

How long a person has had diabetes and how poorly it is controlled are among the most important risk factors: the longer someone lives with the disease, the higher the risk for the kidneys. High blood pressure (hypertension) also plays a key role: it often comes with diabetes and increases the risk of developing chronic kidney disease and of it getting worse. A genetic predisposition has also been observed: kidney disease is more common in people with a family history of it. Although the exact genetic basis is still unknown, family history is very useful when planning prevention and care.

Other factors that often contribute are older age, obesity, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome. These factors not only raise the risk of kidney disease but also worsen the symptoms and complications of diabetes. Finally, lifestyle and environmental factors such as smoking, physical inactivity, and a high-sodium diet can intensify kidney damage, mostly by promoting high blood pressure, inflammation throughout the body, and metabolic problems. Having had an acute kidney injury or another kidney condition has also been linked to a higher chance of developing this disease.

learn.label: Risk factors
learn.title: What you can’t change, and what you can.
learn.author: Jasmyn

paragraphs: The main risk factors for diabetic nephropathy are poor blood glucose control, high blood pressure, how long a person has had diabetes, and genetic predisposition. The combination of these risk factors can work together to worsen kidney health, causing a greater harmful effect than what each factor would cause individually.

columns.title: Can’t be changed
items: Duration of diabetes: the risk increases significantly after more than 10 years with the illness.
Age over 55, which is associated with stiffer blood vessels and kidneys that are more easily damaged.
Higher incidence in African American, Asian, and Native American people.
Genetics: siblings of people who develop diabetic nephropathy have three times the risk.

columns.title: Can be changed
items: Poor diabetes control: high HbA1c levels are linked to a faster loss of the kidneys’ ability to filter (glomerular filtration rate).
Hypertension (high blood pressure), partly due to an overactive renin–angiotensin system.
Albuminuria and proteinuria (protein in the urine).

learn.note: These factors act together and increase the risk of developing diabetic nephropathy.

learn.label: How damage happens
learn.title: How the filter gets damaged.
learn.author: William
steps: Diabetic kidney disease occurs when high blood sugar damages the kidneys over time. This damage can cause inflammation, scarring, and changes in how the kidneys filter blood. One sign is albuminuria, which means protein is leaking into the urine.
High blood sugar can damage kidney cells and cause inflammation and scarring. It can also affect hormones and blood vessels that help the kidneys work properly, eventually leading to kidney damage.

One way diabetes damages the kidneys is by increasing harmful molecules that can injure cells. This can weaken the kidneys’ filters, allowing proteins to pass into the urine. As a result, protein levels in the urine may increase over time.

Diabetes can also cause the kidneys to filter blood harder than normal, increasing pressure inside their tiny blood vessels. Over time, this extra pressure can damage the kidney filters and worsen kidney function.

A hormone system called the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system helps control blood pressure and fluid balance. When this system stays too active, it can increase pressure inside the kidneys and contribute to inflammation and scarring, making kidney disease worse.

As kidney disease progresses, the structures that support the kidney filters can become thicker and develop scar-like changes. These changes make it harder for the kidneys to filter blood properly and can contribute to the gradual loss of kidney function.

Specialized kidney cells that help keep the filters working properly can also become damaged. When this happens, the kidneys may have trouble keeping proteins in the blood, causing more protein to leak into the urine.
In advanced stages, more severe scarring and structural damage can develop inside the kidneys. These changes can further reduce the kidneys’ ability to filter blood and maintain normal function.

learn.label: Clinical signs
learn.title: Silent for years.
learn.draft: ajustado por el equipo de diseño (v4.6), por validar
learn.author: Stephanie

paragraphs: Diabetic nephropathy shows up as albuminuria that increases over time, a decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and, in late stages, swelling of the legs (peripheral edema) and high blood pressure. For much of its course it causes no obvious symptoms.

timeline.title: Glomerular hyperfiltration
timeline.text: The kidneys filter more than normal. It is reversible, causes no symptoms, and usually appears in the early stages.

timeline.title: Microalbuminuria
timeline.text: The first sign of diabetic nephropathy. It usually causes no symptoms.

timeline.title: Macroalbuminuria
timeline.text: May develop after years of untreated microalbuminuria. It may come with a progressive rise in blood pressure.

timeline.title: Falling GFR
timeline.text: Once macroalbuminuria is established, filtration falls progressively.

timeline.title: End-stage kidney disease
timeline.text: The most advanced stage. How long it takes to get there varies a lot from person to person, and treatment can delay or prevent it.

after: This is a general model, not a prognosis: not everyone goes through every stage or at the same pace, and some people have reduced filtration without albuminuria.
Swelling of the legs is usually the first symptom people notice before seeking care, but it appears at a very advanced stage of the disease.

Diabetic nephropathy is also linked to other complications: high blood pressure, which tends to worsen as the disease progresses, and more illness and death from cardiovascular causes, because people with a low GFR and high albuminuria have much higher rates of kidney failure, hospitalization, and death. It is also often associated with diabetic retinopathy (eyes) and large-vessel disease, as well as neuropathy, bladder problems, cognitive impairment, and depression. This is why diabetic nephropathy is a hub for many diabetes complications.
pro: Glomerular hyperfiltration corresponds to a higher-than-normal GFR; more than 120 mL/min/1.73 m² is often used as a reference.
Assessment for microalbuminuria or macroalbuminuria is recommended in people with diabetic retinopathy and macrovascular disease.

learn.label: Diagnosis
learn.title: How it’s confirmed.
learn.draft: ajustado por el equipo de diseño (v4.6), por validar
learn.author: Brady

paragraphs: The diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy depends on the type of diabetes, how well it is controlled, how it has progressed, the signs and symptoms, and other factors.

Regular measurements should be taken, and clinical findings should be related to kidney disease: glucose measurements and laboratory results are considered together with the person’s signs and symptoms. In type 1 diabetes, if albuminuria (albumin in the urine) appears less than 5 years or more than 25 years after diagnosis, the kidney disease is less likely to be caused by diabetes. These time frames guide the health team but do not decide the cause on their own. People with type 2 diabetes, on the other hand, may already have diabetic nephropathy when their diabetes is diagnosed.

The main damage comes from injury to small blood vessels caused by sustained high glucose. This affects not only the kidneys but other organs too, which is why people with diabetic nephropathy may also have diabetic retinopathy (eyes) and diabetic neuropathy (nerves). The diagnosis is usually clinical: it combines symptoms, physical examination findings, and laboratory results. A kidney biopsy is not needed in most cases; it is considered in specific situations, for example when the picture is not typical or another cause is suspected.

learn.proTitle: What a biopsy can show under light microscopy
pro: Extracellular matrix deposits, primarily in the mesangium.
Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane.

learn.label: Prevention
learn.title: Protecting the kidneys.
learn.author: Victoria

paragraphs: Preventing diabetic kidney disease (DKD) involves managing diabetes and reducing the risk of kidney damage. The main strategies are controlling blood sugar, managing high blood pressure, detecting kidney problems early, and reducing other risk factors.

cards.title: Blood sugar under control
cards.text: Keeping blood sugar under control is one of the most important ways to prevent kidney damage. For most adults with diabetes, the recommended HbA1c is around 7% or lower. HbA1c is a blood test that measures average blood sugar over the past two to three months. This goal can change depending on a person’s age and overall health. For people with type 1 diabetes, starting insulin treatment early can help prevent kidney disease.

cards.title: Early detection
cards.text: Early detection is one of the most important tools. Urine tests check for albumin, a protein that can appear when the kidneys are damaged, and blood tests measure kidney function. They are recommended yearly for type 2 diabetes and from five years after diagnosis for type 1 diabetes. To confirm persistently high albumin, at least two out of three urine tests taken over three to six months must be abnormal. Abnormal results should be confirmed with repeat testing, because infections, exercise, and high blood sugar can temporarily affect them.

cards.title: Blood pressure
cards.text: For people with DKD, the recommended blood pressure is generally below 130/80 mmHg, when safe. Doctors may prescribe medications called ACE inhibitors or ARBs to lower blood pressure, which reduce kidney damage, especially when protein is found in the urine. They should not be taken together and are not recommended solely for prevention in people with normal blood pressure and kidney function.

cards.title: Additional medications
cards.text: For people with type 2 diabetes who already have kidney disease, additional medications can help slow kidney damage: SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and finerenone. Treatment depends on kidney function and overall health. Regular checkups help monitor kidney health and possible side effects, especially after starting or changing medications.

cards.title: Habits
cards.text: Eating a healthy diet, exercising regularly, maintaining a healthy weight, and avoiding smoking can help protect the kidneys. Managing high cholesterol can reduce the risk of heart problems associated with diabetes and kidney disease.

learn.note: Goals and medications are set by your health team. Do not start, change, or stop a treatment on your own.
sources: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee, 2026

faqDescription: Short answers. Each one links to the part of the site that explains it in more detail, and to its source.

faq.q: If I have diabetes, will my kidneys be damaged?
faq.a: Not necessarily. About 2 to 4 in 10 people with diabetes develop diabetic kidney disease. Keeping blood sugar and blood pressure within the goals you agree on with your health team greatly lowers the risk.

Two simple tests: a urine test (albumin-to-creatinine ratio), which looks for protein in the urine, and a blood test (creatinine), used to calculate eGFR. With diabetes they are usually done at least once a year; your health team decides how often.
Almost never at first. It can go years without symptoms. Leg swelling or tiredness show up when the disease is already advanced. That is why tests are the only way to catch it early.

faq.q: Can it be slowed down or reversed?
faq.a: If it is caught early, treatment can slow it down and, in early stages, albumin in the urine can go down. Function that is badly damaged does not come back, but what still works can be protected.
There is no single kidney diet. What suits you depends on your kidney function and your results. The recipes on this site are examples to talk over with your dietitian.

faq.q: Can I take over-the-counter pain relievers?
faq.a: Some common anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen or naproxen, can harm the kidneys if used often or in high doses. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before taking them.

faq.q: When should I see a doctor soon?
faq.a: If you notice new swelling, you urinate much less than usual, you feel short of breath, or you have tiredness that does not get better, see a doctor soon. For severe symptoms, seek emergency care.

learnGuides.key: Diabetic kidney disease is common, but it does not happen to everyone with diabetes.
summary: It appears in about 2 to 4 in every 10 people with diabetes.
In type 2 diabetes it can already be present at diagnosis.
Risk grows with years of diabetes, high blood pressure and other factors.

learnGuides.key: Kidney damage in diabetes has several causes that add up.
summary: High glucose over a long time is the main cause.
High blood pressure often comes with diabetes and speeds up damage.
Family history, tobacco, salt and obesity also play a part.

learnGuides.key: Some factors cannot be changed, but several of the most important ones can.
summary: Cannot be changed: years with diabetes, age, genetics and sex.
Can be changed: glucose, blood pressure, cholesterol, tobacco and weight.
Factors add up: improving one already helps.

learnGuides.key: High glucose and pressure inside the kidney slowly damage the filter.
summary: The kidney filter becomes inflamed and scarred.
Pressure inside the kidney rises and strains the filters.
An early sign is albumin (protein) in the urine.

learnGuides.key: For years it causes no symptoms: that is why it is measured with tests.
summary: At first it only shows up in urine and blood tests.
Swelling and tiredness appear when it is already advanced.
The course is a general model, not a personal prognosis.

learnGuides.key: It is confirmed by combining repeated tests with the clinical history.
summary: A urine test (albumin) and a blood test (creatinine to estimate eGFR) are used.
An abnormal result is repeated before confirming.
A biopsy is not needed in most cases.

learnGuides.key: Controlling glucose and blood pressure and getting timely check-ups protects the kidneys.
summary: Glucose and blood pressure goals are agreed with the care team.
Urine and blood tests are recommended at least once a year.
Not smoking, moving and watching salt all add up.
